prompt: Which sentence does the course use to define the architect?
hint: Three verbs.

choices.text: The most senior programmer on the team, promoted for writing good code
choices.why: That confuses a reward with a job; seniority is not the role.

choices.text: Whoever decides, documents and answers for the structural choices
choices.why: Right: each verb carries part of the job, and answering gives the other two their weight.

choices.text: The person who draws the diagrams
choices.why: That confuses a view with the architecture, which lesson 2 separated.

choices.text: The one who approves every change
choices.why: That describes a bottleneck rather than a role.

prompt: Carreto has 7 teams, so 21 pairs of teams. If it grew to 9 teams, how many pairs of teams could make a decision that affects each other?
In the incident that led Tomás to create the role, Matching and Payments each changed how a load's status was stored. What made it a case for an architect rather than a case of bad engineering?
hint: Each change on its own was reviewed and tested.

choices.text: Neither team had written tests
choices.why: Both changes were tested; the failure lay where they met.

choices.text: Payments' code was older and fragile
choices.why: Age plays no part; two correct changes combined into a wrong result.

choices.text: The tech leads did not get along
choices.why: No conflict between people is described; nobody owned the seam.

choices.text: Both changes were right alone; nobody owned the place they met
choices.why: Right: the seam between teams had no owner, which is the gap the role fills.

prompt: On Thursday of her first week, Kátia asks Renata to decide whether Matching gets its own database. What does Renata do?
hint: She has an opinion, and holds it back.

choices.text: Asks for a week and a page describing the problem
choices.why: Right: answering would show the role does something, but the decision belongs nearer the team, as the next section explains.

choices.text: Says yes, since she knows the shared table's history
choices.why: Knowing the history makes her a source of advice, not the obvious decider.

choices.text: Says no until Payments stops reading loads
choices.why: That was Bruno's advice later on, and Kátia did not take it.

choices.text: Sends the question to Tomás
choices.why: The CTO created the role so that questions at the seams stop climbing to him.

prompt: Renata's Friday page says what the role will not do. Which of these are on it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three refusals.

choices.text: Approve pull requests
choices.why: Yes: approving every change would make her the bottleneck the role is not.

choices.text: Propose owners for open questions
choices.why: That is what the page does: nine open questions, each with a proposed owner.

choices.text: Manage anybody
choices.why: Yes: the architect is not the manager of the engineers whose systems they shape.

choices.text: Decide product priorities
choices.why: Yes: what the product does belongs to product, and lesson 16 draws that line.

prompt: An architect at another company spends every day pairing inside one team's codebase and is rarely seen elsewhere. By the lesson, what has the role become?
hint: The job is at the seams.

choices.text: The ideal: close to the code
choices.why: Closeness to code matters (lesson 15), but one team's code leaves the seams unwatched.

choices.text: That team's senior engineer
choices.why: Right: depth in one place without the view across is a different job.

choices.text: The diagram-drawer from the opening paragraph
choices.why: That is the opposite failure, an architect who never looks at code.

choices.text: A tech lead with formal authority
choices.why: Nothing here is about authority; it is about where the attention goes.

prompt: What is the difference between formal and earned authority, by the lesson?
hint: Who grants each one?

choices.text: Formal is written down; earned is spoken
choices.why: Both can be written down or not; the difference is where they come from.

choices.text: Formal belongs to managers, earned to engineers
choices.why: Renata holds both and manages nobody.

choices.text: The organisation grants one; colleagues give the other
choices.why: Right: the title is granted and can be removed; trust is built team by team and can be spent.

choices.text: Earned authority is the formal kind after a year in the job
choices.why: Time in the job does not convert one into the other; Renata has six years and little trust with Driver.

prompt: What does formal authority alone produce, by the lesson?
hint: Think of a team told what to do by somebody it does not trust.

choices.text: Compliance in the letter, workarounds in practice
choices.why: Right: and teams stop telling the architect things early.

choices.text: Faster decisions with fewer incidents
choices.why: Decisions may be quick, but problems go unreported, which produces incidents rather than preventing them.

choices.text: Influence without a mandate
choices.why: That is the opposite case: earned authority without the title.

choices.text: Open disagreement in the architecture forum
choices.why: Teams under formal authority alone tend to go quiet, not argue in public.

prompt: By the advice process as Harmel-Law describes it, what must somebody do before making an architectural decision?
hint: Two groups to ask.

choices.text: Get the architect's approval
choices.why: The process removes the veto; the architect becomes one source of advice.

choices.text: Reach consensus with every affected team
choices.why: The decider listens and is free not to follow the advice; consensus is not required.

choices.text: Seek advice from those affected and from people with expertise
choices.why: Right: ask and listen, then decide, with no obligation to follow what was said.

choices.text: Present it at the monthly architecture review
choices.why: An open forum supports the process, but the rule is about whom to ask.

prompt: Put the steps of Kátia's decision about Matching's database in order.
hint: Ask, then decide, then write it down.
items: Kátia takes the decision on, as Matching's tech lead
She asks Bruno, the Shipper team and Paula, who are affected
She asks Renata and Paula for their expertise
She decides, and records the advice she did not take
trap: Recording the decision before asking would turn the advice into a formality.

prompt: Kátia follows Renata's advice and not Bruno's. In the advice process, what does that mean for Bruno's advice?
hint: The decider has to hear advice, not follow it.

choices.text: The process failed, since an affected team was overruled
choices.why: Overruling advice is allowed; the obligation is to seek it and listen.

choices.text: Bruno can escalate to Renata, who decides
choices.why: Renata advised; she holds no veto under this process.

choices.text: It is recorded with the reason it was not taken
choices.why: Right: Kátia wrote that the first step touches nothing Payments reads.

choices.text: It no longer counts, since advice is optional
choices.why: Seeking it is the one requirement; what is optional is following it.

prompt: Which of these does the lesson name as a limit of the advice process?
hint: Where does it end?

choices.text: It is slower than one architect deciding everything
choices.why: The lesson argues the reverse: fifty engineers decide in parallel instead of queuing.

choices.text: It moves decisions away from the people with the knowledge
choices.why: It does the reverse, putting Matching's decision with Matching.

choices.text: Two teams deciding incompatible things about one seam
choices.why: Right: the process does not settle that, nor say who answers when a decision fails.

choices.text: Engineers resent advice
choices.why: Advice they were free to decline is the kind nobody resents.

prompt: In a RACI chart, how many people should be accountable for one result?
hint: A result two people answer for...

choices.text: Everyone who did the work
choices.why: Those are the responsible; several are fine, and they are a different letter.

choices.text: Two, so that one can cover for the other
choices.why: Two accountable people means each assumes the other answers.

choices.text: Exactly one
choices.why: Right: several can be responsible, one answers for the result.

choices.text: The whole team, collectively
choices.why: Collective accountability is the case where nobody answers.

prompt: Matching and Payments both believed the way a load's status was stored was theirs to change. What does the lesson call the missing thing?
hint: Who may decide what.

choices.text: Written decision rights
choices.why: Right: a decision right that is not written down is settled by whoever moves first.

choices.text: An architecture diagram of the loads table
choices.why: A diagram shows the table; it does not say who may change it.

choices.text: A code-review rule requiring two approvals
choices.why: Both changes were reviewed; the gap was ownership of the seam.

choices.text: A stronger test suite in Payments
choices.why: Tests in each team passed; nothing tested the combination nobody owned.

prompt: It is three in the morning, payments are failing, and somebody has to choose between two rollbacks now. Where on the lesson's spectrum does the decision belong?
hint: Urgency.

choices.text: The team decides after seeking advice
choices.why: Seeking advice takes time an incident does not have.

choices.text: One person decides alone
choices.why: Right: somebody must decide now, and a meeting is the wrong tool.

choices.text: Architect and teams decide together
choices.why: Deciding together suits a contested seam with time to talk, not a live incident.

choices.text: The team decides and informs the architect later
choices.why: The position is close, but here the urgency, not the team's ownership, is what matters.

prompt: Two drivers were paid twice: R$ 2,850 and R$ 4,100. How many reais had to be recovered in all?
hint: Add the two duplicate payouts.

prompt: In the incident review, what did Renata identify as the real mistake behind the double payouts?
hint: Not the code, and not quite the retry policy.

choices.text: Ícaro's retry code
choices.why: Ícaro wrote exactly what was specified; blaming him would miss the decision.

choices.text: The bank's unclear documentation
choices.why: The review recorded it, but answering for a decision means looking first at your own part.

choices.text: Deciding at position 1 what belonged at position 4
choices.why: Right: deciding alone, to save a meeting, removed the people who would have asked about the key.

choices.text: Using Pix instead of bank transfers
choices.why: The payment method is not the issue; any rail needs duplicates refused.

prompt: Which of these is part of answering for a decision, by the lesson, and not merely taking the blame?
hint: What makes an account useful to the next person?

choices.text: Apologising at length in the review
choices.why: A long apology makes an account contrite, not useful; she spoke briefly and moved on.

choices.text: Offering to step down from the role
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson asks for it; answering is about explaining and changing things.

choices.text: Fixing the code herself that night
choices.why: The fix shipped through the team; what she owned was the decision and the process.

choices.text: Explaining what she knew then
choices.why: Right: what she knew and what she assumed show where the reasoning broke, which makes an account useful rather than contrite.

prompt: The fix for the double payouts was to send an ___ key with every payment request, so the bank refuses a repeated one.
hint: The word for an operation that is safe to repeat.

prompt: Match each decision at Carreto to where it belongs on the lesson's spectrum.
hint: Cost of reversal, teams affected, urgency, knowledge.

pairs.left: choosing a rollback during a live incident
whether Matching gets its own database
pairs.right: the team decides after seeking advice

pairs.left: a logging library inside one service
which team owns the loads table

prompt: A newly appointed architect, unknown to most teams, overrules three teams on her first day to show the role has teeth. What does the lesson predict?
hint: What does each use of the title cost?

choices.text: Teams will respect the role sooner
choices.why: Respect comes from earned authority, which overruling spends rather than builds.

choices.text: Compliance, workarounds, and teams that stop telling her things
choices.why: Right: formal authority alone produces obedience in the letter and an architect who hears about decisions late.

choices.text: Nothing changes, since the CTO publicly backs her and her new role
choices.why: The CTO's backing is formal authority; it does not make anybody tell her things early.

choices.text: Influence without a mandate
choices.why: She has the mandate; what she lacks is the trust.

prompt: After the double payouts, why did Renata's earned authority with Bruno's team rise instead of fall?
hint: What had they expected her to do?

choices.text: The fix shipped within a day
choices.why: It shipped the following Monday, and speed of the fix is not what the lesson credits.

choices.text: Tomás publicly defended her
choices.why: No defence by the CTO is described; the change came from how she behaved.

choices.text: She owned it when they expected her to blame Ícaro
choices.why: Right: the title cannot grow by admitting a mistake, and trust frequently does.

choices.text: The amount lost was small
choices.why: R$ 6,950 is not trivial, and the size of the loss is not what moved the team.

prompt: Why does the lesson say authority and accountability should not be separated?
hint: One combination is a trap; the other is worse.

choices.text: RACI charts require it
choices.why: RACI names who is accountable; the argument here is about what each mismatch does to people.

choices.text: Architects are paid to carry both, and the salary reflects it
choices.why: Pay is not mentioned; the reasons are learning and trust.

choices.text: The advice process forbids it
choices.why: The advice process keeps them together by making the decider answer, but it is not the reason given.

choices.text: Each half without the other fails people
choices.why: Right: blame without the right to decide is a trap, and deciding without answering stops the learning; teams then quietly stop trusting the decisions.
